agent_b_operating_model.summary: Post-700 portfolio ownership is architecturally sound across 4 defined tracks but has 6 ownership gaps that could produce unowned maintenance tasks during maintenance mode. All 4 tracks have clear scope boundaries; the gaps emerge at track interfaces (who owns the handoff, who updates shared baselines, who verifies cross-track compliance).
agent_b_operating_model.verdict: ARCHITECTURE_CLEAN — 6 gaps require resolution before maintenance mode is fully operational
findings: F1 — 100-series (Maintenance): Scope is well-defined (runtime bug fixes, session recovery, app.js integrity) with explicit exclusions (no content changes, no governance decisions). The app.js baseline (SHA-256 5A4338C6... / 209,937 bytes, 2026-07-25) is the authoritative reference point.

F2 — 300-series (Analytics): 8-session trajectory (S302→S309) executed from DQS through Bottleneck Analysis. Produced consumable models (DQS, EQS, BQS, ExQS, UIQS, Risk Register, Forecast Engine). Read-only constraint held across all 8 sessions. S310 (Portfolio Operations Dashboard, 300-series closeout) was recommended by S309 but not yet executed.

F3 — 600-series (Candidate): Evaluated by S309 with DEFER recommendation. Startup cost (3-4 sessions) equals projected savings (3-4 sessions). No existing sessions, files, or artifacts. Pure proposal.

F4 — 800-series (Modernization): S803 cleared for launch (112 items, 9 batches, net +1 Certified). S802 governance correction lane refuted 3 P0 blockers as DL-029 artifacts, compressed roadmap from 19→12 sessions. Proven track record of embedded EW authoring within certification waves.

F5 — Track Scope Clarity: All 4 tracks have well-defined WHAT (scope) and WHAT-NOT (exclusions). The ambiguity is at track interfaces — WHO owns shared resources (CURRENT_BASELINES.md, defect manifest, REVISION_HISTORY.md) when multiple tracks operate on the same packs.
gaps: GAP-B1: CURRENT_BASELINES.md maintenance ownership. After a pack-file write (by 100 for app.js fix, or by 800 for certification), who updates CURRENT_BASELINES.md §2 hash table? The S723 Maintenance Framework nominates a 'Baseline Maintainer' agent type, but no trigger condition defines when this agent should be spawned. If every write session triggers baseline refresh, the 11-entry sparse log (§5 of CURRENT_BASELINES.md) suggests compliance will be inconsistent.

GAP-B2: 300→Maintenance model consumption path. 300-series produced DQS/EQS/BQS/ExQS/UIQS models that were 'consumed by governance.' Post-700 closure, governance is in maintenance mode. The 7 maintenance agent types (Governance Auditor, Reconciliation Agent, Defect Sweeper, Certification Auditor, Baseline Maintainer, Delivery Safety Inspector, Remediation Agent) are defined in the framework but none has an explicit 'consume analytics model' function. If 300-series is re-run (e.g., a new bottleneck analysis), who acts on the results?

GAP-B3: 800-series certification governance verification. When 800 certifies items (S803: 112 items), who enforces G-NEW-1 through G-NEW-5 certification-blocking rules? Under 700-series governance, certification governance was self-contained within the certification wave. Post-700, the maintenance-mode Certification Auditor agent is read-only — it audits but cannot block. The governance guard plugin enforces Rules 1-5 but G-NEW-1 through G-NEW-5 (explanation relevance, dual-block source-of-truth, case explanation sufficiency) are not implemented in the plugin. This gap means 800 could certify items with G-NEW-2 violations (wrong-topic EW text) without automated blocking.

GAP-B4: Defect manifest maintenance after remediation. When 800-series certifies Pack C Section B items and DL-008 is resolved, who updates `governance/DEFECT_MANIFEST_DL008_DL026.json` to remove those QIDs? The manifest was created by May's authoring pipeline and is referenced by CURRENT_BASELINES.md §3 as containing '117 blocked QIDs.' No maintenance agent type has 'update defect manifest' in its scope.

GAP-B5: 300-series S310 dangling closeout. S309's session summary states 'Recommended next: S310 — Portfolio Operations Dashboard (300-series closeout).' This session has not executed. The 300-series is left open-ended — its final deliverable (the dashboard) is unconsumed by any downstream process. If S310 is never executed, does the 300-series remain in an open (not-closed) state analogous to the 700-series closure? The portfolio has two overlapping analysis lanes (300 analytics, 700 calibration — now in maintenance) and no formal series lifecycle management.

GAP-B6: May coaching layer ownership. The May coaching layer (may-core.js 344,883 bytes, may-learner-state.js 110,240 bytes) provides hints, defect-aware recommendations, and exam-mode gates. It is included in CURRENT_BASELINES.md as a runtime-critical file. It is referenced by app.js (G4 hint-count integration at line 1431). It was developed in sessions S120–S131. But no track owns May: 100 is maintenance (bug fixes), 300 is analytics (read-only), 600 is candidate (doesn't exist), 800 is certification. Who governs May's defect-aware recommendation logic? Who ensures May's hint database stays current with content changes? This is a runtime-critical component with zero owning track.
agent_b_operating_model.recommendation: The 4-track portfolio architecture is sound and the track boundaries are well-defined. Do not refactor. Address the 6 gaps as follows: (1) Assign CURRENT_BASELINES.md updates to the session that performs writes — the writer is responsible for baseline refresh, enforced by the governance guard's Rule 1 WARN cascade. (2) Define 300-series as 'on-demand' — spawn only when pre-delivery safety checks or periodic deep audits indicate a need, not on a fixed schedule. (3) Add G-NEW-1 through G-NEW-5 as governance guard rules (or as a separate pre-certification validation script) before any 800-series certification wave executes. (4) Delegate defect-manifest updates to the Remediation Agent as a mandatory post-remediation verification step. (5) Execute S310 as the formal 300-series closeout to close the open analysis lane. (6) Assign May coaching layer ownership to the 100-series (since it is a runtime dependency, not content) with 'read-only on content, write-only on bug fixes' scope identical to app.js.

agent_c_maintenance_readiness.summary: The S723 Maintenance Framework is architecturally complete — 5 cadence tiers, 6 trigger thresholds, 4 escalation conditions, 7 agent types — but is not operationally executable at present. Three CRITICAL blockers (stale baselines, DL-029-vulnerable guard detection, undefined session cadence tracking) mean a new operator following the framework would produce unreliable results or miss real defects. The framework succeeds as a specification but not as an executable playbook.
agent_c_maintenance_readiness.verdict: CONDITIONALLY_READY — 3 CRITICAL blockers must be resolved before the framework can be trusted for operational use
findings: F1 — Audit Cadence Architecture: The 5-tier cadence (T0 entry, Rapid Pulse, Deep Audit, Pre-Delivery Safety, Baseline Refresh) covers the full maintenance lifecycle. Each tier has defined checks and a time budget. The escalation path from any tier to trigger thresholds is logically coherent. The concept is well-designed — graduated intensity with time-sensitivity gating.

F2 — Trigger Thresholds: The 6 thresholds cover the key failure modes discovered in the 700-series (certified count drift from DL-019, DL-008 re-emergence from DL-013 overwrites, guard failures, pack parse corruption from DL-017, hash drift from concurrent-write, CC distribution skew). Severity grading (CRITICAL→HIGH→MEDIUM) is correctly calibrated against actual observed failure impact.

F3 — Escalation Conditions: 3 of 4 conditions are correctly gated. The DL-008 re-emergence condition correctly gates at ≥1 (any re-emergence is CRITICAL). The new-defect condition correctly gates at severity ≥ HIGH. The answer-key integrity condition correctly gates at TIER 1 audit level. The certified-count regression condition points to 300-series reconciliation but should point to the Reconciliation Agent instead (see gap C5).

F4 — Maintenance Agent Types: The 7 agent types are well-scoped with read-only/write permissions clearly indicated. The distinction between 'Governance Auditor' (read-only, T0 protocol) and 'Reconciliation Agent' (read-only, G1-G5 gates) provides separation of concerns. The 'Remediation Agent' (the only write agent for pack-file fixes) correctly requires BLOCK-AUTHORIZED marker and ≤30 items/batch cap — the governance guard's Rule 5 provides automated enforcement.
gaps: GAP-C1 (CRITICAL): Governance guard DL-008 detection uses DL-029-vulnerable ±1200 char window. The S723 Maintenance Framework states: 'DL-008 Function constructor parse' as the T0 check. The actual governance guard plugin (`.opencode/plugins/governance-guard.js`) still uses forward-scan from ExplanationWrong matching CorrectChoice within a window — the same method that produced ~75% false positives across S700-S800. S723 Operational Readiness §repeatability.gaps explicitly flags this: 'The plugin can produce false positives when CC is >1200 chars from EW.' S802's 8 Permanent Prevention Rules mandate Function-constructor parse ONLY. The framework's tooling does not match the framework's specification. Impact: A new operator following the T0 protocol would run governance guard tests (20/20 PASS on synthetic data), see a clean result, and fail to detect real DL-008 because the plugin's window-scan missed it — or would see false-positive DL-008 and escalate unnecessarily. Both outcomes are dangerous.

GAP-C2 (CRITICAL): CURRENT_BASELINES.md §3 (Defect & Risk Status) is stale — lists 67 Certified DL-008 items as CRITICAL despite S802 proving 0 actual. The T0 entry protocol checks 'Certified count grep' against baselines, and any delta >5 triggers HIGH escalation. A new operator would read the stale defect status from CURRENT_BASELINES.md, see the claimed 67 Certified DL-008, and immediately trigger emergency remediation — perpetuating the false-alarm cascade that S802 was created to stop. The framework depends on CURRENT_BASELINES.md as the single source of truth, but that document has not been updated to reflect S802's findings. The 6 COND conditions from S723 Operational Readiness (specifically COND-1 and COND-2, both CRITICAL) remain unresolved.

GAP-C3 (CRITICAL): No session counting mechanism. The Rapid Pulse cadence triggers 'Every 5 sessions or 3 hours of write activity.' Neither condition can be measured with existing tooling: (a) Session numbering (S309, S530, S723) is informal — no registry, no counter, no automated increment between sessions. An operator must manually count sessions since the last Rapid Pulse. (b) '3 hours of write activity' requires tracking cumulative write-agent time across sessions — no mechanism exists. The framework assumes stateful session tracking that the repository's tooling doesn't provide. Impact: Rapid Pulse cadence would be inconsistently applied — most likely skipped because monitoring it requires manual bookkeeping nobody is formally assigned to.

GAP-C4 (HIGH): Escalation destination for DL-008 re-emergence is circular. The framework states: 'DL-008 re-emergence (≥1 Certified) → 700-series emergency remediation.' But the 700-series is CLOSED (per S723 Program Closure Report). There is no active 700-series to receive this escalation. The Remediation Agent (7th in the maintenance agent list) could handle it, but: (a) the Remediation Agent is the only write agent with ≤30 items/batch cap — a full DL-008 remediation could span dozens of batches, (b) the escalation condition doesn't name the Remediation Agent, it names a closed program. A new operator following the escalation path would look for '700-series emergency remediation' and find only the closed program — with no instructions on how to proceed.

GAP-C5 (HIGH): '13 runtime hashes' cannot be mapped to CURRENT_BASELINES.md's 15 files. The framework requires checks against '13 runtime hashes' at T0/Tmid/Tend. CURRENT_BASELINES.md lists 15 files: 3 app core, 2 May layer, 5 MCQ packs, 5 scored cases. Which 2 files are excluded? S723 Operational Readiness §repeatability.gaps flags: 'The 13 runtime hashes referenced in AGENTS.md §13.1 does not map cleanly to CURRENT_BASELINES.md which lists 15 files. Which 2 are excluded? Not documented.' The Framework inherits the same ambiguity. Impact: Hash verification at T0 would either verify 13 of 15 files (missing 2 that might be runtime-critical) or verify all 15 (breaking the '13' cardinality expected by downstream checks).

GAP-C6 (MEDIUM): Deployment definition missing. Pre-Delivery Safety triggers 'Before any learner-facing deployment.' The simulator is a single-page application with no CI/CD pipeline, no versioned releases, no staging environment, and no deployment process. Changes to pack files or app.js take effect immediately when the page is reloaded. There is no 'deployment' event to trigger the check. Does Pre-Delivery Safety run after every pack-file write? After every app.js change? On a calendar schedule? The framework provides no concrete trigger signal.

GAP-C7 (MEDIUM): No automated trigger monitoring. All 6 trigger thresholds require manual operator initiation — there is no script that auto-scans on session open, detects threshold violations, and reports results. The T0 entry protocol instructs the operator to run specific checks, but framework compliance depends on the operator remembering to execute all checks. With 15 files to hash-verify, 5 packs to parse-count check, DL-008 to Function-constructor verify, and governance guard 20/20 to run, the ~5 minute time budget is optimistic for a manual process. Recommendation COND-5 from S723 (automated baseline verification script) would reduce this to ~30 seconds but has not been implemented.
agent_c_maintenance_readiness.recommendation: Do not activate the maintenance framework in its current state. Execute 3 pre-activation actions: (1) Fix the governance guard's DL-008 detection to use Function-constructor parse (per S802 Prevention Rules). Until this is done, the T0 DL-008 check is unreliable and could produce false positives that trigger unnecessary CRITICAL escalations. (2) Update CURRENT_BASELINES.md §3 to remove the 67 Certified DL-008 items (proven 0 by S802) and reconcile all stale state with the S723 closure baseline — per COND-1 and COND-2 from S723 Operational Readiness. (3) Create `scripts/t0_baseline_verify.js` as recommended by S723 COND-5 — this single script would automate the T0 entry protocol's 5 checks and reduce the time budget from ~5 minutes manual to ~30 seconds automated. Without this script, the T0 protocol's compliance rate will be low. Post-activation, the framework is operationally viable.

agent_d_charter_review.summary: The 600-series charter defines clean separation from 300 (analytics), 700 (governance), and 800 (certification) at the conceptual level. The separation is architecturally coherent: 300 observes, 600 drafts, 700-governs, 800 certifies. However, S309's DEFER recommendation remains correct — and is now stronger than when it was made. The post-S802 bottleneck reduction (DL-008=0, 67 phantom items cleared, 7 sessions saved from roadmap) means the workload that 600 would accelerate is smaller than S309 assumed. Additionally, 4 charter gaps (output mechanism, quality gate authority, case-bank scope, May integration) would need resolution before any launch.
agent_d_charter_review.verdict: DEFER REAFFIRMED — separation is architecturally clean but launch is not justified. S309 conditions still hold. If reevaluated, 4 charter gaps should be closed first.
findings: F1 — 300/600 Separation: CLEAN. 300-series is read-only analytics producing quality scores and models (DQS, EQS, BQS, ExQS, UIQS). 600 would produce content artifacts (EW text, templates, distractor libraries). No overlap in output type or authority. The boundary is: 300 reports what quality exists; 600 creates content to improve quality. One unidirectional dependency: 600 should consume 300 analytics to inform authoring priorities (e.g., 'which distractor patterns perform worst?') — this is a consumption path, not an authority conflict.

F2 — 700/600 Separation: CLEAN. 700-series (now maintenance mode) governs certification standards (CAQS, DCS, G-NEW rules) and enforces governance guard rules. 600 produces draft content only — no certification, no recalibration, no governance decisions. The boundary is: 600 creates drafts that are candidates for governance review; 700/maintenance-mode governance decides what gets certified.

F3 — 800/600 Separation: CLEAN IN CONCEPT. 800 certifies items using CAQS §1.6 six-dimension verification. 600 drafts explanation content. The boundary is: 600 authors EW/EC text; 800 reviews, certifies, and writes to pack files. However, as S309 noted, 800-series certification already embeds EW authoring — there is currently no handoff. Adding 600 would CREATE a handoff that doesn't exist today. This is not a boundary violation but a process inefficiency.

F4 — S309 Analysis Confirmed and Strengthened: The S309 DEFER recommendation was based on: startup cost (3-4 sessions) ≈ projected savings (3-4 sessions) → net NEUTRAL. Post-S802, the bottleneck has shrunk: DL-008=0 freed 3 sessions, 67 phantom items cleared, roadmap compressed from 19→12 sessions. The remaining 800-series workload is smaller and the embedded EW authoring in certification waves has proven adequate (S537 ENHANCED_CASE_BASE: 42 explanations expanded in a single session, all Certified). The 600-series becomes even LESS necessary under the reduced workload.
gaps: GAP-D1: No defined output mechanism. The charter says 600 drafts EW, EC expansions, and templates. But these outputs must eventually be written into pack files to be consumed by the runtime engine. How does 600's output reach the pack files? Three possible models, none defined: (a) 600 writes directly to pack files (triggers backup protocol, governance guard rules, baseline refresh — 600 would need write authorization and batch-cap compliance), (b) 600 writes to separate 'draft' files that 800 imports during certification (adds file management complexity, potential for sync issues akin to DL-019 concurrent-write), (c) 600 operates purely in-memory/chat and the operator manually applies the output to pack files (error-prone, no audit trail). Until an output mechanism is defined, the charter is a workflow concept, not an executable plan.

GAP-D2: Quality gate authority is ambiguous. The EW Factory Model (SESSION309_EW_FACTORY_MODEL.json, Agent O) defines 4 stages: Draft → Review → Technical QA → Certification Candidate. Stage 3 'Technical QA' includes automated scans (DL-008 check, empty-slot check, boilerplate check, minimum-length check). This effectively duplicates governance's certification checks before certification happens. If 600's QA passes but 800's certification review finds issues: (a) does 600 re-draft or does 800 fix? (b) Is 600's QA binding (800 trusts it and skips redundant checks) or advisory (800 re-verifies everything)? The charter says '600 would NOT certify' but the EW Factory Model gives 600 certification-like QA powers. This ambiguity could lead to governance gaps where items certified by 800 rely on 600's QA that missed defects.

GAP-D3: Case-bank scope undefined. The charter describes 'Content Operations' (EW factory, rewrite preparation, template systems, standards libraries) and 'Authoring Infrastructure' (distractor libraries, misconception maps, explanation templates). It does not specify whether these apply to MCQ items only (pack_*_corrected.js) or also to case-bank items (scored_cases*.js). The S309 analysis identified 298 Domain C case-bank items with 'near-zero EW' — a natural 600-series target if launched. But case items have different EW requirements (exhibit-dependent reasoning, multi-step calculations, business-context interpretation) than MCQ items. The charter's template systems would need separate templates for case vs. MCQ — a complexity not addressed.

GAP-D4: May coaching layer integration not planned. If 600 drafts new EW text, the May coaching layer (may-core.js, which provides hints and defect-aware recommendations) would need to reference updated EW content. May's hint database and recommendation logic currently operate on the existing EW text. 600-drafted EW could introduce new content that May's coaching doesn't recognize, producing gaps in hint coverage. No integration path between 600 drafts and May's content-indexing logic is defined.

GAP-D5: Re-evaluation criteria are underspecified. S309 says 'Re-evaluate after 800-series Waves 2-3 if authoring velocity proves to be the actual bottleneck.' Waves 2-3 is ambiguous — S803 (112 items, 9 batches) is presumably Wave 1. How many waves does the 800-series have? The 700-series closure report lists residual items including Pack C/D E/F certification (400 items uncertified) and DL-026 (100+ EW fields). If 800-series completes all remaining certification in 4-5 waves, the re-evaluation point would be at Wave 3 — approximately 2-3 sessions from now. But if the 17-session expected timeline (from S309) holds, the re-evaluation point might be 8-10 sessions out. Without a concrete wave-count target, the re-evaluation is deferred indefinitely.
agent_d_charter_review.recommendation: REAFFIRM DEFER. The 600-series charter has clean conceptual separation across all tracks but the business case has weakened since S309. Post-S802 bottleneck reduction means the 800-series can complete remaining certification without a separate drafting lane. If the 600-series is ever re-evaluated: (1) resolve GAP-D1 (output mechanism) — define whether 600 writes to pack files, draft files, or operates in-memory, (2) resolve GAP-D2 (quality gate authority) — declare 600's QA as advisory only, with 800 holding final certification authority, (3) specify case-bank vs. MCQ scope explicitly, (4) plan May coaching layer integration for any newly authored EW text, (5) set concrete re-evaluation criteria: 'After 800-series Wave 3 (estimated 5-7 sessions from S724) if per-session EW authoring throughput falls below 50 items/session.' Current throughput (S537: 42 explanations in one session) already approaches the factory model's projected 50 items/session — the efficiency argument for a factory lane is weak.
